h1: Brewing two batches back to back on one brew day
title: Brewing Two Batches on One Brew Day | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew two batches back to back on one homebrew day: the kit you need, a staggered timeline, cleaning between beers and where it goes wrong.
teaser: Two beers for one day of set-up and cleaning. Here is the timeline that makes a double brew day work.
standfirst: Setting up and cleaning take a large share of every brew day. Brewing two batches back to back spreads that time over twice the beer. It works if you stagger the steps and plan the kit before you start.
sections: Why brew twice in one day

A typical all-grain brew in a bag day runs five to six hours. A good part of that is setting up, heating water and cleaning. Brewing two batches back to back shares that overhead. A well-planned double day takes eight to nine hours rather than ten to twelve for two separate days.

It also makes comparison easy. Two beers brewed on the same day with the same water and the same malt lot are a fair test of anything you change between them, such as a hop or a yeast.

The trick is staggering: batch two mashes while batch one boils. That needs two heat-tolerant vessels.

  • Two vessels: a kettle for boiling and a second pot, cooler or mash tun for mashing. An insulated cool box makes a good mash tun.
  • Two heat sources, or one big enough to heat strike water while the boil runs. A single induction plate makes a double day very slow.
  • Two fermenters, cleaned and ready, plus yeast for both.
  • Enough cooling. An immersion chiller and a supply of cool water, or two ice baths ready.

If your kit only allows one vessel at a time, a double day still works, but it becomes two brews in a row with less saving.

Here is a workable plan for two 20 litre brew in a bag batches with a separate mash vessel:

  • 0:00 heat strike water for batch one.
  • 0:45 mash batch one, 60 minutes. Start heating water for batch two.
  • 1:45 lift the bag, start heating to a boil.
  • 2:15 mash batch two in the second vessel. Batch one boils for 60 minutes.
  • 3:15 chill batch one, transfer and pitch.
  • 3:45 move batch two's wort into the kettle and bring to the boil.
  • 4:15 to 5:15 boil batch two. Clean batch one's kit during the boil.
  • 5:15 to 6:30 chill batch two, transfer, pitch and clean up.

Times stretch on a domestic stove. Write your own timeline the night before and keep it on the counter.

Total up water for both batches before you start. Two 20 litre brew in a bag batches can need 60 to 65 litres in total, so a storage drum and enough Campden tablet or RO water to cover it saves a scramble. Weigh and bag both grain bills the night before, labelled clearly.

Cooling is the usual bottleneck. Indian tap water in summer can be 28 to 30 °C, which limits how cold a chiller can get the wort. A final ice bath or a pre-chiller coil in a bucket of ice water helps reach pitching temperature. Plan for ice for two batches, not one.

After the boil, the wort can be infected. Anything that touches batch one's cooled wort should be cleaned and sanitised again before it touches batch two. That includes the siphon, the jug, the hydrometer jar and your hands. On a long day, sanitiser in a bucket goes weak with dirt, so make up fresh for the second batch.

Label fermenters with the beer and the date as you fill them. After eight hours on your feet, two fermenters of amber wort look exactly the same.

Fatigue makes mistakes. Brew the beer with the trickier recipe first, while you are fresh. Leave the forgiving one for second. If one beer has heavy late hops or a lot of dark malt, consider brewing it second as well, so any residue left in shared kit ends up in the bolder beer.

Yeast needs planning too. If you use dry yeast, have two sachets ready. If one batch uses liquid yeast, make its starter a day or two ahead so it is at full strength when the wort is ready. Pitching batch two late because the starter was not ready leaves warm wort sitting unprotected, which is exactly what you want to avoid in Indian heat.

Eat, drink water and take a break during the second mash. Skipped hop additions and forgotten yeast are classic second-batch errors. Tick each step on a printed brew sheet.
Split batches are the easier first step

If a full double day sounds like a lot, start with a split. Brew one bigger batch and divide it, as in our guides to splitting wort between two yeasts and comparing two dry hops. You get two beers for one mash and one boil. Once that feels easy, add the second mash. Your first all-grain brew day notes will tell you how long each step actually takes on your system.

Your first step: time each stage of your next normal brew day, then sketch a staggered plan using your own numbers.
faqs: How long does a double brew day take?
A well-planned double all-grain day takes about eight to nine hours, compared with ten to twelve for two separate days.
What extra kit do I need to brew two batches in a day?
A second mash vessel, enough heat to run a boil and heat water at the same time, two fermenters and enough cooling for both.
Which beer should I brew first?
Brew the more demanding recipe first while you are fresh. Brew the bolder beer second if kit is shared.
